title: MCPs are Boring (or: Why we are losing the Sparkle of LLMs) - Manuel Odendahl

primary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations

summary: Manuel Odendahl, a 25-year software engineering veteran coding with LLMs since the 2022 Copilot alpha, critiques the current state of MCPs and tool calling as boring and restrictive. He observes a paradox: LLMs are excellent at coding—they can one-shot entire applications and know recently built APIs—yet they remain poor at function calling, seemingly stuck at GPT-3.5 intelligence levels. He argues code itself is a tool: SQL queries are code, and LLMs can write code that calls tools, runs agents, and recurses infinitely at inference time. Rather than constraining LLMs with static tool schemas, he proposes eval as the only MCP needed. LLMs can create, modify, and reuse tools on demand—like magical genies. A SQL eval example demonstrates this: when asked about John Smith's orders, the LLM discovers tables, inspects schemas, writes a join with aggregation, and returns a deterministic, reusable query for about 500 tokens versus 5,000 tokens and wrong arithmetic via traditional tool calling. Once a query works, it can be stored as a SQL view, eliminating future schema lookups. Building libraries (import star from CRM) replaces MCP servers; LLMs handle 10,000 API functions well in code but struggle with the same as tool calls. He references the Voyager paper and 'code elicits better tool actions.' Generated code can build rich UIs via a UI DSL rendered by the host application—sliders, dropdowns, file attachments, scroll views with filters—replacing primitive JSON edit windows. His sandbox.js MCP prototype in Go with SQLite and web server libraries demonstrates eval saving tool calls and tokens. The demo culminates in a complete CRM: the LLM generates 15 functions, REST API endpoints, and website handlers for JavaScript, CSS, and HTML—all from a single eval call in 2-3 seconds instead of 15 tool calls. The resulting CRM is fully functional without the LLM, allowing users to edit and add companies stored in a database. Odendahl closes by advocating recursive thinking—asking LLMs to write code, then to write code that writes code—creating self-referential libraries reusable across systems. He emphasizes that engineers and LLMs are both engineers; everything is engineering. LLMs are absolute magic, far more than structured tool-call emitters, and we should reclaim their sparkle.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Introduction
sections.summary: Manuel Odendahl introduces himself as a 25-year software engineering veteran, embedded engineer, and backend/database enthusiast. He has been coding with LLMs since the 2022 Copilot alpha and shares tips on his Program With AI Twitter account.

sections.title: Tool Calling Fundamentals
sections.summary: Explains that LLMs are language producers trained on tool-calling content, enabling structured output that maps to function/API/MCP calls without explicit schemas. Demonstrates the standard flow with a weather query: LLM receives tool schemas, selects a tool, deterministic code executes, LLM re-inferences on results.

sections.title: MCP Possibilities and Problems
sections.summary: MCP allows any LLM app to use tools built by others, but problems emerge: too many tools cause selection confusion; arguments must be inferenced by the LLM, repeating context already present; full JSON results waste tokens. CRM example shows 36 companies, 20,000 tokens, 50 cents, 5-minute wait when only an email is needed.

sections.title: Why MCPs Are Restricted and Boring
sections.summary: Argues MCPs don't leverage LLM capabilities fully. Proposes passing chat history, memories, and file metadata to tools for argument reuse and context-aware calls. Notes security and protocol design challenges across different modalities. References 90s/2000s work on ontologies, semantic web, XML schemas.

sections.title: UI Improvements for Tool Calls
sections.summary: Advocates for richer user interaction: editing tool arguments before execution and editing results before they re-enter the LLM. Demonstrates with an overdue-invoices SQL query featuring approve/reject/edit dialogues. Notes this is faster and cheaper than LLM processing.

sections.title: LLMs Are More Than Tool Callers
sections.summary: Concludes by emphasizing LLMs are versatile language producers trained on everything, capable of adopting any persona or format based on prompting. Hints at deeper explorations including context editing beyond the talk's scope.

sections.title: Code as Tool and the Eval Proposal
sections.summary: Observes the paradox that LLMs one-shot entire applications and know recently built APIs yet remain poor at function calling, seemingly stuck at GPT-3.5 intelligence. Argues code is a tool (SQL is code), and LLMs can create tools on demand like magical genies. References the Voyager paper and 'code elicits better tool actions.' Proposes eval as the only MCP needed, noting coding agents already do most work via bash calls.

sections.title: SQL Eval Example: Dynamic Tool Creation
sections.summary: Demonstrates eval with SQL: asked about John Smith's orders, the LLM discovers tables, inspects schemas, writes a join with aggregation. Uses ~500 tokens and returns deterministic, reusable query versus 5,000 tokens and wrong arithmetic via traditional tool calling. Once working, the query can be stored as a SQL view for future reuse, eliminating repeated schema discovery.

sections.title: Libraries Instead of MCPs
sections.summary: Argues that creating reusable functions and views constitutes a library. Instead of exposing a GitHub MCP, give eval access to a preconfigured GitHub library. LLMs handle 10,000 functions well in API/code form but struggle with the same as tool calls. Proposes import star from CRM instead of building MCP servers, enabling LLMs to create custom tools with loops and rich logic.

sections.title: UI-Rich Tool Interactions via DSL
sections.summary: Proposes that generated code can build UIs via a DSL rendered by the host application—sliders, dropdowns, file attachments, scroll views with filters—replacing primitive JSON edit windows. Users can validate, tweak, attach files, save preferences, and recall tools by modifying previous inputs.

sections.title: Sandbox.js Prototype Demo
sections.summary: Demonstrates a Go-based sandbox.js MCP with SQLite and web server libraries and a single eval call. The LLM writes JavaScript that filters tables in code rather than streaming all results back, saving two tool calls and tokens. Shows execute.js for loading pre-written files, with the LLM filtering and querying in a single flow.

sections.title: Full CRM from a Single Eval Call and Recursive Creation
sections.summary: The sandbox.js demo concludes with the LLM generating 15 functions, REST API endpoints with registered handlers, and a complete website with JavaScript, CSS, and HTML handlers—all from a single eval call in 2-3 seconds instead of 15 tool calls. The resulting CRM is fully functional without the LLM: users can edit and add companies stored in the database. Odendahl advocates recursive thinking—asking LLMs to write code, then to write code that writes code—creating self-referential libraries reusable across systems. He emphasizes that engineers and LLMs are both engineers; everything is engineering, not just tool calling. He closes by urging the audience to reclaim the sparkle and magic of LLMs, which are far more than structured tool-call emitters.
